summary: AstroVitals is a web-based health self-assessment tool for astronauts on long-duration missions, built by Team TAKA. On Mars-distance missions, messages take about 20 minutes each way, so crews must spot health problems themselves. AstroVitals lets an astronaut log eight indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood, loneliness and exercise). It shows them on a clickable body map with green, amber and red status, adds trend charts, instructions for taking each measurement, and guidance on what to do next. Each indicator is linked to NASA Human Research Program hazards such as gravity fields and isolation. Timed reminders cover water, supplements and exercise. A mental health section offers guided breathing, a daily connection plan, a private journal, and a motivation screen with the astronaut’s goals and family photos when stress is high. A simulated Mission Control link sends reports and an emergency alert, and the crew can request a mission abort review. Astronaut health, physical and mental, decides mission success, so tools like this help crews act early. Demo data is simulated.
details:
What it does and how it works
AstroVitals is a web app that helps astronauts assess their own health on long missions, when help from Earth can be about 20 minutes away each way. The astronaut logs eight indicators: resting heart rate, blood pressure, fasting blood sugar, body temperature, sleep, mood, loneliness and daily exercise. Each reading is checked against a normal range and shown as green, amber or red on a clickable body map. Selecting an indicator shows how to measure it, why it matters in space, which NASA Human Research Program hazards it relates to, and what to do at each level. Trend charts show 14 days of readings against the normal range. A readiness score, points, streak and level keep the crew engaged.

Reminders alert the astronaut to drink water, take supplements as prescribed, exercise, measure vitals, check mood, rest and connect with someone. A simulated Mission Control link sends reports, with signal delay shortened for the demo. If overall health becomes critical, an emergency alert is sent automatically and the astronaut can request a mission abort review, with a confirmation step. The decision itself stays with the flight director and commander.

Mental health and isolation
The tool includes guided breathing, a daily connection plan, messages home queued for the next downlink, a private journal, an isolation risk check, and a support request to the behavioral health team. When stress is high, a motivation screen shows the astronaut’s own goal, mission message, family photos and favorite song next to one action to take. Personal items stay on the device and are not sent in reports.

Benefits and intended impact
Crews can detect problems early, act without waiting for Earth, and keep flight surgeons informed when needed. Treating mental health as a core vital sign addresses a risk that is easy to neglect. The same approach could support remote clinics, polar stations and other isolated teams on Earth.

Creativity
The design assumes autonomy first, because of the communication delay. It combines physical and mental health in one view, uses the body map as the main interface, and shows personal motivation at the moment of highest stress.

Factors we considered
Which indicators can really be measured in space, how NASA’s five hazards affect them, clear color coding for non-experts, privacy of personal content, and keeping a human decision-maker in charge of any mission abort. Limitations: the demo data is simulated, the Mission Control link is a simulation, the ranges are general adult reference values, and the app is a prototype, not a medical device. Flight surgeons would need to set crew-specific baselines.

Tools and technology
HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page with no external libraries, using browser storage for local data. Design and planning drew on NASA’s Human Research Program five hazards and on records from ISRO’s Axiom-4 mission and NASA’s Open Science Data Repository and ISS Environmental Data Application. We used Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, to help generate the app’s code and wording.
